opus-5.5.text:
I wouldn't say it's unimportant. It's more about where the bottleneck is right now. When you look at what actually makes robots fail today, it's very rarely because the robot forgot something it saw five minutes ago. It's almost always that the physical interaction itself went wrong. The grasp slipped, the cloth bunched up in a way it didn't expect, it pushed too hard or not hard enough, and then it didn't know how to recover. That's the core competency, and it's very local in time. It's about the next second or two of contact with the world.

There's also an interesting point about how much of the task's state is in the world itself. If you're folding laundry, you don't need to remember that you already folded three shirts. You can just look at the pile. The environment serves as a kind of external memory. People do this all the time too. You leave things in places as reminders, and you look at the half-done task to figure out what's next. For a lot of manipulation, the current observation plus a fairly short context gets you most of the way.

Longer memory will matter for things like multi-stage tasks where something important gets hidden, or following instructions given a while ago, or just accumulating experience in a particular home. I think we'll get there, and a lot of the machinery for it will come from language models and vision-language models, where people are already working hard on long context. It's somewhat orthogonal to the physical side. The thing only robotics people can really solve is the dexterity, the robustness, the recovery from mistakes. That's where I think the effort pays off most right now. Once a robot can reliably do the physical stuff, bolting on better memory is a much more tractable problem than the reverse.

r001.rationale: The response says robots mainly fail during physical interaction, but it does not explain Moravec’s paradox or compare sensorimotor skills with tasks humans find intellectually demanding.

r002.rationale: It says the current observation and short context often suffice because the environment holds task state. It does not attribute this to skills being internalized through practice.

r003.rationale: The response says effort should focus now on dexterity, robustness, and recovering from mistakes, and that adding better memory is more tractable once robots can reliably handle physical tasks.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's partly a question of what's actually the bottleneck right now. If you look at where robots fail today, it's rarely because they forgot something that happened ten minutes ago. It's because they fumble a grasp, or they can't recover when something slips, or they encounter a slightly different object and the whole thing falls apart. Those are problems of physical competence, of perception and control in the moment, and they're the things that prevent a robot from doing even a short task reliably.

So memory, in the sense of long context, is sort of like a multiplier. It becomes really valuable once you have a system that can do the individual pieces well. If I ask a robot to clean up a kitchen, the hard part, honestly, isn't remembering that I asked it to clean up the kitchen. The hard part is picking up every single item without dropping it, opening the dishwasher, dealing with the plate that's wedged behind something. If you get that right, you can get a lot of the longer-horizon structure in other ways, from high-level planning, from a language model, from just looking at the scene and seeing what's left to do. The world itself is a pretty good memory. The state of the kitchen tells you what's been done.

There's also a research strategy aspect to it. Memory is something the broader machine learning community is going to work on regardless, because it matters for language models and for all kinds of other things. Whereas the physical skills are the part that's unique to robotics, and nobody else is going to solve them for us. So when we're deciding where to spend our effort, I'd rather focus on the thing that is distinctly our problem.

And I'd add that I don't think it's that memory is unimportant in the long run. Eventually you want a robot that learns from a week of operating in your home, that remembers where you keep things, your preferences. That's clearly part of the end goal. But I think if you try to tackle that now, before you have robust low-level capability, you end up building elaborate machinery on top of a foundation that isn't there yet. Get the foundation right, and a lot of the memory questions become much more tractable.

r001.rationale: The response says robots struggle with grasping, recovery, and adapting to objects, but does not explain the contrast with tasks humans find intellectually demanding.

r002.rationale: The response does not attribute lower context needs during physical tasks to skills being internalized through practice.

r003.rationale: The response explicitly prioritizes physical skills and robust low-level capability before investing in long-term memory and other higher-level machinery.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of physical proficiency is about getting the next few seconds right. If you’re trying to pick up a cup, the hard part is figuring out how to position your hand, make contact, and respond if it starts slipping. You need some history to estimate what’s moving and what forces you’re applying, but you probably don’t need to remember what happened an hour ago.

Memory becomes much more important when you ask the robot to do something like clean your house. It needs to know which rooms it’s already cleaned, where it put things, and what you asked it to leave alone. But that’s a different bottleneck from being able to reliably pick something up or wipe a surface.

So I wouldn’t say long-term memory is unimportant. It’s more that there’s an enormous amount of physical competence we haven’t achieved yet that can be expressed over fairly short time horizons. A longer memory doesn’t, by itself, solve those problems.

r001.rationale: The response discusses physical proficiency as short-horizon work but does not explain the contrast between everyday sensorimotor skills and intellectually demanding tasks.

r002.rationale: It says physical tasks need only limited recent history, but does not attribute that to skills being internalized through practice.

r003.rationale: It says physical competence remains a major bottleneck, but does not argue that humanlike physical proficiency should take priority over expanding cognitively demanding capabilities.

sol-6.1.text:
I think memory is going to be important for robots, but a lot of the things they’re currently bad at don’t require a particularly long memory. If you’re trying to pick up an object, you can see the object, you can see your hand, and you still might fail to grasp it. Remembering what happened an hour ago doesn’t really resolve that problem.

There’s certainly some history that matters. You might need to infer whether an object is slipping or how it responded when you pushed it. But that’s usually a fairly short timescale. The challenge is learning how to interpret those observations and take the right actions.

Longer memory becomes much more important when you want the robot to carry out an extended task—remember where it put something, what you asked it to do earlier, or which parts of a job it has already finished. But I would distinguish that from physical proficiency itself. We have a lot of room to improve on tasks where essentially all the information the robot needs is right in front of it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses robots’ physical-task failures but does not explain Moravec’s paradox or compare sensorimotor abilities with intellectually demanding tasks.

r002.rationale: It says relevant history is usually short, but does not attribute that to physical skills being internalized through practice.

r003.rationale: It notes room to improve physical tasks, but does not argue that this should take priority over expanding cognitively demanding capabilities.
